title: Real-life phrases with rise and fall
purpose: Play with rise and fall in phrases you really use, and find a melody that feels like you.
instructions: Jot down a few short phrases you say a lot.
Say them with a little more movement in your voice than usual, so they sound livelier.
Lean on the words that carry the meaning.
Then try longer things you'd really say.
Record and listen back, and keep what feels like you.

primary_cue.text: Let the melody follow what you mean.

cues.text: Let the melody follow what you mean.
Add a little more rise and fall, then listen back.
Lean only on the words that carry the meaning.

practice_task.prompt_text: Are you coming tonight? I'd love that, thank you!

check_questions.text: Did the rise and fall fit what you meant, and feel like you?

expected_observations: Lively speech moves more than pitch: loudness, pace and your face all change a little too.
common_misunderstandings: You don't need an exaggerated melody, an accent or particular words. Overdoing it while you explore can help you find your range; that part is optional.
stop_conditions: Anything hurts, feels tight or scratchy, or your voice turns hoarse: that usually means too much, too soon.
Rest your voice and come back another day, starting smaller.

Hoarseness that lasts more than about three weeks, sudden voice loss or pain needs a GP or primary care doctor, who can have your vocal folds looked at. A speech and language therapist who works with voices can help with technique.
adaptations: Swap the example phrases for your own.
limitations: Written for Lilt for practising on your own. Lilt can't check your technique, and it doesn't replace a speech and language therapist.
Lilt doesn't judge whether your intonation is right. A sentence that falls at the end isn't wrong.
